events.title: NeXTstation released
events.summary: NeXT began shipping the NeXTstation in September 1990 — a more affordable Motorola 68040 workstation running NeXTSTEP.
events.about: The NeXTstation dropped the cube's magneto-optical drive for a conventional SCSI hard disk and color display — putting NeXTSTEP in more university labs and startups. Developers still used Objective-C and Interface Builder; Tim Berners-Lee's WWW work continued on NeXT hardware. Apple later acquired NeXT and ported NeXTSTEP to become macOS.

narrative.whyChosen: The NeXTstation made NeXTSTEP workstations accessible beyond the original cube's price point.
narrative.whyImportant: It spread the development environment that became the foundation of modern macOS and iOS tooling.
narrative.problemSolved: The original NeXT Computer was too expensive for many research groups that wanted NeXTSTEP.

events.title: Archie search engine launched
events.summary: Alan Emtage launched Archie in September 1990 at McGill University — the first tool for indexing FTP archives across the internet.
events.about: Archie crawled anonymous FTP servers and let users search filenames before the web existed — a direct ancestor of Yahoo, Google, and every search box. It proved the internet needed discovery layers on top of raw protocols.

narrative.whyChosen: Archie was the first internet search engine.
narrative.whyImportant: It showed indexed discovery was essential as networked files exploded.
narrative.problemSolved: FTP servers multiplied; users could not manually find files across hosts.
